children.translated_text: The supernatural powers such as divine descent, flying vehicles, flywhisks, and other splendors—

children.text: māyāviṣvapi dṛśyante nātastvamasi no mahān // SAm_1 //
children.translated_text: are seen even in magicians; therefore, you are not great to us because of these.
This great display of forms and such, both internal and external,

children.text: divyaḥ satyo divaukassvapyasti rāgādimatsu saḥ // SAm_2 //
children.translated_text: divine and real, exists even among celestial beings who possess <s>rāga</s> (attachment) and other passions.
Due to mutual contradiction among the doctrines of the <s>Tīrthaṅkaras</s> (ford-makers),
not all of them possess trustworthiness; only someone indeed can be the true teacher.
The complete elimination of faults and obscurations exists through supreme excellence,
just as somewhere the destruction of inner and outer impurities occurs through their own causes.
Just as subtle, hidden, and distant objects become directly perceptible to someone,
and fire and such are inferred [by others]—thus is the establishment of the omniscient one.
You alone are faultless, whose words do not contradict reason and scripture;

children.text: avirodho yadiṣṭaṃ te prasiddhena na bādhyate // SAm_6 //
children.translated_text: non-contradiction is established if your doctrine is not refuted by what is well-known.
For those outside the nectar of your doctrine, the absolutist proponents of all kinds,
burnt by false pride in their own trustworthiness—their own positions are refuted by experience.
Wholesome and unwholesome <s>karma</s> and the next world would not exist at all
among those devoted to one-sided views, O Lord, who are enemies to themselves and others.
In the absolutism of existence, through the denial of the non-existence of entities,
[everything would be] of the nature of all, beginningless and endless, without own nature—[a conclusion] not belonging to your [teaching].
The effect-substance would be beginningless if prior non-existence is denied,

children.text: pradhvaṃsasya ca dharmasya pracyave 'nantatāṃ vrajet // SAm_10 //
children.translated_text: and if the destructive cessation of a property is removed, it would go on endlessly.
That one thing would be of the nature of everything if the exclusion of the other is transgressed;
it would be designated in every way as inherent in other things.
Even in the absolute non-existence position, of those who deny existence,

children.text: bodhavākyaṃ pramāṇaṃ na kena sādhanadūṣaṇam // SAm_12 //
children.translated_text: instructive speech and <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid knowledge) would not exist—by what then would proof and refutation be made?
Due to contradiction, the identity of both is not possible for those hostile to the logic of <s>syādvāda</s>;
and in the absolutism of inexpressibility too, the statement 'it is inexpressible' is not logically tenable.
In some respect, it is accepted as existent; in some respect, it is indeed non-existent;
likewise, both, and inexpressible—but through proper reasoning, not in every respect.
Who would not accept that everything exists, from the fourfold standpoint of own nature and so forth?
It is non-existent from the opposite standpoint—if not, it would not be distinguishable.
From the two [existence and non-existence] attributed successively, duality arises; simultaneously, it is inexpressible due to the incapacity of language;
the remaining three modes have 'inexpressible' as their component, each from its own cause.
Existence, being invariably concomitant with the negated in one subject,
serves as a qualifier establishing agreement, when difference is intended to be expressed.
Non-existence, being invariably concomitant with the negated in one subject,
serves as a qualifier establishing disagreement, when non-difference is intended to be expressed.
The qualified subject, whose nature comprises both the affirmed and the negated, is the object of language;
just as the property to be proved is both a cause and a non-cause depending on the standpoint.
The remaining modes are also to be understood according to the reasoning stated above;

children.text: na ca kaścidvirodho 'sti munīndra tava śāsane // SAm_20 //
children.translated_text: and there is no contradiction at all, O best of sages, in your teaching.
"Through affirmation and negation thus, the agent of purpose becomes unsettled"—
this objection is invalid, for according to the task at hand, external and internal conditions determine which mode applies.
With respect to each property, the meaning is different for the property-bearer possessing infinite properties;
when one viewpoint becomes the principal aspect, the remaining viewpoints become subordinate to it.
One should apply this procedure regarding the alternatives of one and many in subsequent topics as well;
one skilled in <s>nayas</s> (viewpoints) should apply this sevenfold procedure through the viewpoints.
Even in the absolute non-duality position, the observed difference creates a contradiction;
one thing does not produce itself from itself, nor do agents and actions [arise from a single source].

children.text: karmadvaitaṃ phaladvaitaṃ lokadvaitaṃ ca no bhavet /
children.translated_text: There would be no duality of <s>karma</s> (action), no duality of fruit, no duality of worlds;
there would be no pair of knowledge and ignorance, nor the pair of bondage and liberation.
If non-duality is established through a reason, there would be duality between the reason and what is to be proved;

children.text: hetunā cedvinā siddhirdvaitaṃ vāṅmātrato na kim // SAm_26 //
children.translated_text: if it is established without a reason, would not duality exist merely from speech?
Non-duality cannot exist without duality, just as a non-cause cannot exist without a cause;

children.text: saṃjñinaḥ pratiṣedho na pratiṣedhyādṛte kvacit // SAm_27 //
children.translated_text: the negation of a conscious being cannot occur anywhere without something to be negated.
Even in the absolute separateness position, since separateness is not separate from itself,

children.text: pṛthaktve na pṛthaktvaṃ syādanekastho hyasau guṇaḥ // SAm_28 //
children.translated_text: there would be no separateness in separateness, for that quality resides in many [loci].
Continuum, aggregate, similarity, and unrestricted
afterlife—none of these would exist if unity is denied.

children.text: sadātmanā ca bhinnaṃ cejjñānaṃ jñeyād dvidhā 'pyasat /
children.translated_text: If knowledge, being of the nature of existence, is different from the knowable, then knowledge is in two ways non-existent;

children.text: jñānābhāve kathaṃ jñeyaṃ bahirantaśca te dviṣām // SAm_30 //
children.translated_text: in the absence of knowledge, how can the knowable exist, whether external or internal, for those who hold such antagonistic views?
The words of others convey only general meaning; particulars cannot be expressed;
due to the non-existence of universals for them, all their words are entirely false.
Due to contradiction, the identity of both is not possible for those hostile to the logic of <s>syādvāda</s>;
and in the absolutism of inexpressibility too, the statement 'it is inexpressible' is not logically tenable.
Without mutual dependence, both separateness and unity would be unreal, since both would lack a cause;

children.text: tadevaikyaṃ pṛthaktvaṃ ca svabhedaiḥ sādhanaṃ yathā // SAm_33 //
children.translated_text: that very unity and separateness, through their own distinctions, serve as the means of proof.
From the universal of being, there is unity of all; from the distinction of separate substances and so forth, there is difference;
in the expression of difference and non-difference, it is like an uncommon reason.
The intention to express and the intention not to express, regarding the qualified subject possessing infinite properties—
[apply] to an existing qualifier here, not to a non-existing one, by those who seek that meaning.
Difference and non-difference, being within the scope of <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid knowledge), are not merely conventional;
they are non-contradictory in one subject, through the intention of expressing them as secondary or primary.
Even in the absolute permanence position, change cannot be accounted for;

children.text: prāgeva kārakābhāvaḥ kva pramāṇaṃ kva tatphalam // SAm_37 //
children.translated_text: there would be no agents of action in the first place—where then is <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid knowledge), and where its result?
If the permanent entity is made manifest by the agents of valid knowledge, just as sense objects are manifested,

children.text: te ca nityaṃ vikāryaṃ kiṃ sādhoste śāsanādbahiḥ // SAm_38 //
children.translated_text: and if those are permanent, what can be changed? O virtuous one, those who hold this view are outside your teaching.
If the effect exists in every respect already, it cannot arise, just as a man who already exists need not be born again;
and the theory of <s>pariṇāma</s> (transformation) contradicts the absolute permanence position.
Meritorious and sinful actions would not exist, the afterlife—whence the fruit?

children.text: bandhamokṣau ca teṣāṃ na yeṣāṃ tvaṃ nāsi nāyakaḥ // SAm_40 //
children.translated_text: Bondage and liberation would not exist for those of whom you are not the leader.
Even in the absolute momentariness position, afterlife and such are impossible;
due to the absence of recognition and the like, there can be no undertaking of action—whence then the fruit?
If the effect is non-existent in every respect, let it not arise, like a sky-flower;
let there be no regularity of material cause, and no assurance in the production of effects.
The relation of cause and effect and so forth would not exist, since there is no continuity due to being-other;
like another continuum, a single continuum of moments would be disconnected, being separate from that previous moment.
This word 'non-other' applied to what are in fact others is conventional—how can it not be false?

children.text: mukhyārthaḥ saṃvṛtirnāsti vinā mukhyānna saṃvṛtiḥ // SAm_44 //
children.translated_text: Convention does not have primary meaning; and without the primary, there can be no convention.
Since the fourfold alternative cannot logically be stated in any absolutist position,
identity, difference, and inexpressibility exist between them—between the continuum and its possessor.
Let not even the fourfold alternative of the inexpressible be stated;
for what is beyond all absolutist positions would be non-real, without qualified and qualifier.
Negation of an existing conscious being occurs by means of the intervening nature of substance and so forth;

children.text: asadbhedo na bhāvastu sthānaṃ vidhiniṣedhayoḥ // SAm_47 //
children.translated_text: the difference of the non-existent is not a positive entity, but the entity is the locus of both affirmation and negation.
That which is non-real would be inexpressible, devoid of all absolutist positions;
a real entity itself becomes unreal through the reversal of the procedure.
If all absolutist positions are inexpressible, then what further speech is there about them?
And if this is said to be conventional, it is entirely false, being the opposite of ultimate reality.
Is something inexpressible due to inability of speech, or due to non-existence, or due to non-cognition?

children.text: ādyatoktidvayaṃ na syātkiṃ vyājenocyatāṃ sphuṭam // SAm_50 //
children.translated_text: From the first, the other two statements would not hold—let it be stated clearly without pretense.
That which is without intention harms; that which has proper intention does not harm;

children.text: badhyate taddvayāpetaṃ cittaṃ baddhaṃ na mucyate // SAm_51 //
children.translated_text: the mind devoid of both becomes bound, and once bound, is not liberated.
Since destruction is causeless in this view, the cause of harm is not the harmer;
and the destruction of the mental continuum would constitute liberation, not liberation caused by the eightfold path.
If the combination of causes is for producing a dissimilar effect,
this combination, being non-different from its bases, would be like something unjustified, due to lack of distinction.
The <s>skandhas</s> (aggregates) and continuums, being merely conventional, are unconditioned;
persistence, arising, and decay would not exist for them, like a rabbit's horn.
Due to contradiction, the identity of both is not possible for those hostile to the logic of <s>syādvāda</s>;
and in the absolutism of inexpressibility too, the statement 'it is inexpressible' is not logically tenable.
It is permanent, because of recognition and because its continuity does not cease without cause;
it is momentary, because of temporal distinctions and due to the flaw that cognition does not traverse all.
As a universal, it neither arises nor perishes—this is evident from continuity;
as a particular, it perishes and arises—existing simultaneously with origination and the like in one entity.
The arising of the effect and destruction are causes, by restriction, distinct from the defining characteristic;
they are not independent, due to being situated in birth and the like states—not like sky-flowers.
One who desires gold from a pot or a crown,
experiences grief, joy, and indifference with cause in its destruction, production, and persistence. || SAm_59 ||

children.text: payovrato na dadhyatti na payo 'tti dadhivrataḥ /
children.translated_text: One who has vowed to consume only milk does not eat curds; one who has vowed to consume only curds does not eat milk;
one who has vowed to abstain from cow products consumes neither — therefore, reality is of threefold nature. || SAm_60 ||
If the difference of effect and cause, the otherness of quality and qualified,
and the otherness of the universal from its instances are held absolutely, || SAm_61 ||
then one thing cannot have multiple occurrences because it lacks parts; or if there are many, due to having parts,
it would lack unity — the defect of occurrence would apply to the undeserving. || SAm_62 ||
Even in particular place and time, occurrence would be like conjunction of separate entities;
there would be no co-location of material cause and effect. || SAm_63 ||
Due to the relation of support and supported, there is no independence for things in <s>samavāya</s> (inherence);

children.text: ityayuktaḥ sa sambandho na yuktaḥ samavāyibhiḥ // SAm_64 //
children.translated_text: thus that relation is illogical, nor is it established by those who hold <s>samavāya</s>. || SAm_64 ||
Since universals and <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) are each complete in every instance,

children.text: antareṇāśrayaṃ na syānnāśotpādiṣu ko vidhiḥ // SAm_65 //
children.translated_text: they cannot exist without a substratum — in cases of destruction and production, what is the rule? || SAm_65 ||
There is in every way a non-connection of universals and <s>samavāya</s>;

children.text: tābhyāmartho na sambaddhastāni trīṇi khapuṣpavat // SAm_66 //
children.translated_text: the object is not connected through them — those three are like sky-flowers. || SAm_66 ||
If atoms are held to be absolutely non-different, then even in aggregation, as with separation,
there would be non-aggregation — the four elements would be mere illusion. || SAm_67 ||
From the illusion of the effect follows the illusion of the atom, for the cause is inferred from the effect;
from the non-existence of both, what resides in them — quality, universal, and the rest — also does not exist. || SAm_68 ||
If they are identical, one of the two would be absent; the absence of what remains follows from their inseparability;
there is also contradiction with the number 'two' — and if you say this is merely conventional, that is simply false. || SAm_69 ||
Due to contradiction, identity of both is impossible for those hostile to the logic of <s>syādvāda</s>;
and even in the absolute position of inexpressibility, the statement 'it is inexpressible' is not logically consistent. || SAm_70 ||
The unity of <s>dravya</s> (substance) and <s>paryāya</s> (mode) is established from their non-separation;
and from particular transformation, from the nature of capacity in what possesses capacity. || SAm_71 ||
And from the distinction of name and number, from the distinction of individual characteristics,
and from the difference of purpose and so forth — their difference is not in every respect. || SAm_72 ||
If their establishment is relative, then the two do not stand independently;
and if their establishment is non-relative, then there is no distinction of universal and particular. || SAm_73 ||
Due to contradiction, identity of both is impossible for those hostile to the logic of <s>syādvāda</s>;
and even in the absolute position of inexpressibility, the statement 'it is inexpressible' is not logically consistent. || SAm_74 ||
The inseparability of attribute and attribute-bearer is established through mutual consideration;
for the own-nature of this is not known from itself, like the limbs of agent and indicator. || SAm_75 ||

children.text: siddhaṃ ceddhetutaḥ sarvaṃ na pratyakṣādito gatiḥ /
children.translated_text: If everything is established through reasoning, there is no recourse to perception and the like;
if everything is established through scripture, then even mutually contradictory doctrines would be valid. || SAm_76 ||
Due to contradiction, identity of both is impossible for those hostile to the logic of <s>syādvāda</s>;
and even in the absolute position of inexpressibility, the statement 'it is inexpressible' is not logically consistent. || SAm_77 ||
When the speaker is not authoritative, what is to be established through reasoning is established by reason;
when the speaker is authoritative, what is to be established through his words is established by scripture. || SAm_78 ||
If one holds the absolute position of internal reality alone, cognition and speech are entirely false;
all is mere semblance of valid knowledge — without valid knowledge, how can anything be established? || SAm_79 ||
If the cognition of what is to be proved and the proof is mere <s>vijñaptimātratā</s> (consciousness-only),

children.text: na sādhyaṃ na ca hetuśca pratijñāhetudoṣataḥ // SAm_80 //
children.translated_text: then there is neither what is to be proved nor a reason — due to defects in thesis and reason. || SAm_80 ||
If one holds the absolute position of external reality alone, from the denial of false cognition,
all those who assert contradictory meanings would achieve their goals. || SAm_81 ||
Due to contradiction, identity of both is impossible for those hostile to the logic of <s>syādvāda</s>;
and even in the absolute position of inexpressibility, the statement 'it is inexpressible' is not logically consistent. || SAm_82 ||
With respect to internal objects of knowledge, the denial of false cognition results;

children.text: bahiḥprameyāpekṣāyāṃ pramāṇaṃ tannibhaṃ ca te // SAm_83 //
children.translated_text: with respect to external objects of knowledge, valid knowledge and its semblance are established for them. || SAm_83 ||
The word '<s>jīva</s>' (soul) has an external referent, because it is a designation, like the word '<s>hetu</s>' (reason);
and the designations of illusion such as <s>māyā</s> and the like have referents, just as liberation comes from understanding <s>māyā</s> and the like. || SAm_84 ||
Those three designations — cognition, word, and meaning — express cognition and the rest;
the three understandings of cognition and the rest are similar, being reflections of them. || SAm_85 ||
The utterance, understanding, and valid cognition of speaker, listener, and knower are distinct;
valid cognition applies only in the case of non-error; in error, the two external referents are of such and other kinds. || SAm_86 ||
The validity of cognition and word applies when an external referent exists or does not;
thus the determination of truth and falsehood is logically consistent with respect to the attainment and non-attainment of objects. || SAm_87 ||
If the accomplishment of objects is from <s>daiva</s> (fate) alone, how can fate arise from human effort?
If from fate alone, there would be no liberation — human effort would be fruitless. || SAm_88 ||
If accomplishment is from <s>pauruṣa</s> (human effort) alone, how can human effort arise from fate?
If from effort, it would be infallible — effort exists in all beings alike. || SAm_89 ||
Due to contradiction, identity of both is impossible for those hostile to the logic of <s>syādvāda</s>;
and even in the absolute position of inexpressibility, the statement 'it is inexpressible' is not logically consistent. || SAm_90 ||
With respect to what is not preceded by intention, the desirable and undesirable is from one's own <s>daiva</s> (fate);
with respect to what is preceded by intention, the desirable and undesirable is from one's own <s>pauruṣa</s> (effort). || SAm_91 ||

children.text: pāpaṃ dhruvaṃ pare duḥkhātpuṇyaṃ ca sukhato yadi /
children.translated_text: If for others, <s>pāpa</s> (sin) certainly arises from suffering and <s>puṇya</s> (merit) from happiness,
then even the non-sentient and the passionless would be bound on account of those conditions. || SAm_92 ||

children.text: puṇyaṃ dhruvaṃ svato duḥkhātpāpaṃ ca sukhato yadi /
children.translated_text: If <s>puṇya</s> (merit) certainly arises from one's own suffering and <s>pāpa</s> (sin) from happiness,
then the dispassionate sage, being wise, would be bound by both on account of those conditions. || SAm_93 ||
Due to contradiction, identity of both is impossible for those hostile to the logic of <s>syādvāda</s>;
and even in the absolute position of inexpressibility, the statement 'it is inexpressible' is not logically consistent. || SAm_94 ||
If pleasure and pain, present in oneself or another, are causes of purification and defilement,
then the influx of <s>puṇya</s> (merit) and <s>pāpa</s> (sin) is logically established — if not, your concept of the <s>Arhat</s> is meaningless. || SAm_95 ||
If bondage is certainly from ignorance, then since objects of knowledge are infinite, there is no <s>kevalin</s> (omniscient one);
if liberation comes from a small amount of knowledge, then from much ignorance it would be otherwise. || SAm_96 ||
Due to contradiction, identity of both is impossible for those hostile to the logic of <s>syādvāda</s>;
and even in the absolute position of inexpressibility, the statement 'it is inexpressible' is not logically consistent. || SAm_97 ||
Bondage is from ignorance arising from delusion, not from ignorance in one free from delusion;
liberation would come from a small amount of knowledge arising from the absence of delusion — otherwise one would be deluded. || SAm_98 ||
The varied world arises from desire and the like, in accordance with the bondage of <s>karma</s>;

children.text: tacca karma svahetubhyo jīvāste śuddhyaśuddhitaḥ // SAm_99 //
children.translated_text: and that <s>karma</s> arises from its own causes — the <s>jīvas</s> (souls) are subject to it through purity and impurity. || SAm_99 ||
Purity and impurity are furthermore capacities, like the capacity for being cooked and not being cooked;
their manifestations have a beginning though the capacities are beginningless — their own-nature is beyond the scope of reasoning. || SAm_100 ||
Knowledge of reality, which is your valid means of knowledge, simultaneously illuminates everything;
and the knowledge that arises sequentially is refined by the method of <s>syādvāda</s>. || SAm_101 ||
Equanimity is the fruit of the former; for the latter, the cognition of acceptance and rejection is the fruit;

children.text: pūrvaṃ vājñānanāśo vā sarvasyāsya svagocare // SAm_102 //
children.translated_text: or first, the destruction of ignorance for all this in its own domain. || SAm_102 ||
In sentences, the particle '<s>syāt</s>,' illuminating <s>anekānta</s> (non-absolutism), is a qualifier with respect to what is to be understood;
through connection with meaning, it belongs even to your <s>kevalins</s> (omniscient ones). || SAm_103 ||
<s>Syādvāda</s> — what is its procedure with consciousness, given the absolute position of every standpoint?
Dependent on the method of <s>saptabhaṅga</s> (sevenfold predication), it distinguishes what is to be rejected and accepted. || SAm_104 ||
Between <s>syādvāda</s> and <s>kevalajñāna</s> (omniscient knowledge), both illuminating all reality,
the difference is direct and indirect knowledge — otherwise one of them would be without substance. || SAm_105 ||
Through similarity with what shares the same property as what is to be proved, from non-contradiction,
a <s>naya</s> (standpoint) indicates the particular meaning analyzed by <s>syādvāda</s>. || SAm_106 ||
The aggregate of <s>nayas</s> (standpoints), applications, and absolute positions across the three times —
the unfailing connection of existents — shows that one <s>dravya</s> (substance) exists in many ways. || SAm_107 ||
If an aggregate of falsities is false, we do not hold absolute falsity;

children.text: nirapekṣā nayā mithyā sāpekṣā vastu te 'rthakṛt // SAm_108 //
children.translated_text: <s>nayas</s> independent of each other are false — when coordinated, they accomplish the meaning of reality for you. || SAm_108 ||
The meaning is determined by a statement, through prescription or prohibition;
it is necessarily so and otherwise — otherwise there would be indistinctness. || SAm_109 ||
Reality is both 'this' and 'not this' — speech teaches that it is just this;

children.text: na satyā syānmṛṣāvākyaiḥ kathaṃ tattvārthadeśanā // SAm_110 //
children.translated_text: if it were not true, how could there be teaching of the nature of reality through false statements? || SAm_110 ||
The nature of speech is the unrestricted negation of the meaning of other speech;

children.text: āha ca svārthasāmānyaṃ tādṛgvācyaṃ khapuṣpavat // SAm_111 //
children.translated_text: and if it expresses only its own general meaning, then what is expressed would be like a sky-flower. || SAm_111 ||

children.text: sāmānyavāgviśeṣe cenna śabdārthā mṛṣā hi sā /
children.translated_text: If general speech relates to a particular, word-meanings are not false — for that claim would itself be false;
through the attainment of the intended particular, the '<s>syāt</s>'-qualification is the mark of truth. || SAm_112 ||
What is to be enjoined is a component of the desired meaning, which contradicts prohibition;
just so is the nature of what is to be accepted and rejected — this is the foundation of <s>syādvāda</s>. || SAm_113 ||
Thus this <s>Āptamīmāṃsā</s> has been composed by one desiring the good,
for the understanding of the particular meaning of correct and incorrect teachings. || SAm_114 ||
Victorious in the world is he who is the moon dispelling the darkness of the proliferation of afflictions,
the sun of <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid knowledge) and <s>naya</s> (standpoints) that dispels the darkness of one-sided absolute positions;
the Lord of ascetics, whose splendor, unapproachable, illumines the drops of the ocean of doctrines —
the various rival sectarians worship according to their own partial doctrines. || SAm_115 ||
